in_text_mentions: On presentation, she was haemodynamically stable. Emergency CT of the abdomen and pelvis confirmed a superficial abdominal wall injury with no evidence of intra-abdominal penetrating injury. Incidentally, imaging demonstrated a 12 cm encapsulated left adrenal lesion containing fat, soft tissue, and calcification, with appearances consistent with a giant adrenal myelolipoma (Figure 1). An additional 10 mm right adrenal nodule was also noted incidentally, measuring 17 HU on unenhanced CT.

in_text_mentions: A repeat MRI scan showed that the mass had increased in size to 12.0 × 10.9 cm, and had become more heterogeneous. Her case was discussed in our endocrine multidisciplinary meeting. in_text_mentions: ent underwent bilateral adrenalectomy in April 2021. The removal of both adrenal masses proceeded without complications. The patient received stress hydrocortisone both pre- and post-surgery and continued with a regular dose of hydrocortisone at 50mg four times a day. The gross pathological examination illustrated bilateral adrenal gland masses consisting of bright-yellow adipose-like tissue with hemorrhagic foci, measuring 11x9.5 cm (left adrenal gland mass) and 9x5 cm (right adrenal gland mass). Microscopic examination revealed bilateral myelolipoma with no evidence of malignancy (Figure 2).

A: Panel A is a low-power H&E section of a human adrenal myelolipoma showing the classic admixture of mature adipose tissue and hematopoietic elements within a encapsulated tumor. B: Panel B is a high-power H&E view showing trilineage hematopoietic cells including megakaryocytes, characteristic of adrenal myelolipoma. C: Panel C shows the lipomatous component of a human adrenal myelolipoma with compressed attenuated adrenal cortex at the periphery, indicated by arrows. D: Panel D is an H&E section of adrenal myelolipoma demonstrating tumor adjacent to adrenal cortex, marked with asterisks.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: IHC (CD61) panel showing megakaryocytes admixed with mature adipose tissue in the patient's retroperitoneal mass, supporting the myelolipoma histology (adipose plus hematopoietic tissue) described in the caption and in-text as EAML. [raw subtype: extra-adrenal] B: IHC (CD20) panel showing lymphoid aggregates within the myelolipomatous mass; part of the trilineage hematopoietic component of the lesion. [raw subtype: extra-adrenal] C: IHC (CD71) panel showing erythroid precursors admixed with fat vacuoles, consistent with the hematopoietic component of myelolipoma. [raw subtype: extra-adrenal] D: IHC (MPO) panel showing scattered myeloid cells in the lesion, completing the trilineage hematopoietic evidence for myelolipoma. [raw subtype: extra-adrenal]

in_text_mentions: gs. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a stable pituitary gland with no evidence of a recurrent tumor. Given his concerning constitutional symptoms, a malignancy workup was initiated. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a heterogeneous fat-containing left retroperitoneal mass measuring 6.3x7.0x8.8 cm (Fig. 1) with concerning features for liposarcoma, including the apparent encasement of the left ureter. Additional incidental findings included cystic pancreatic lesions and a right renal lesion, both recommended for further evaluation.

panels.rationale: Single gross pathology photograph of a resected human adrenal myelolipoma, with caption explicitly identifying a well-encapsulated yellow-tan adrenal gland with myelolipoma and in-text confirming surgical resection and pathology. The giant hemorrhagic presentation is a less common variant.
panels.attribution_text: Zulia et al. A Rare Case of Hemorrhagic Giant Adrenal Myelolipoma: Radiographic and Pathologic Correlation.. Cureus 2021. doi:10.7759/cureus.17353. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 8.
panels.figure_caption: Gross Image of Well Encapsulated Yellow-Tan Adrenal Gland with Myelolipoma The myelolipoma measures 760g, 15.2 x 14.0 cm.
in_text_mentions: gh attenuation (Figures 1-3). The mass appeared to arise from the right adrenal fossa displacing the right kidney inferiorly. Subsequent MRI of the abdomen with and without gadolinium confirmed a large, predominantly fat-containing, right adrenal mass with marrow elements and areas of hemorrhage (Figures 4-7). The patient underwent surgical resection, and the post-operative pathology revealed a 760 g well-encapsulated giant hemorrhagic adrenal myelolipoma with fibrosis, and areas of old and fresh hemorrhage (Figures 8-13). The patient is currently disease free and undergoing routine follow-up.

In this case the diagnosis was confirmed with MRI. in_text_mentions: Macroscopic examination revealed a gray-yellow, encapsulated, irregularly shaped mass, 16.5 x 15 x 6.5 cm in size (Figure 4). On cut section, the tumor had fatty appearance and elastic texture. Microscopically, the tumor consisted of mature adipocytes admixed with hematopoietic components, including myeloid, erythroid and megakaryocytic elements (Figure 5). On tumor’s total periphery, there were sites of compressed, normal adrenal tissue, and this finding was similar to the intraoperative appearance of the tumor (Figure 6). These findings confirmed the diagnosis of AML.

visual

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Macroscopic photographs show a fat-containing adrenal tumor with yellow adipose areas and a hemorrhagic cut surface, consistent with adrenal myelolipoma. B: H&E photomicrograph shows adipose vacuoles and cellular hematopoietic elements in the tumor, consistent with myelolipoma, though the caption only calls it a neoplasm. C: H&E photomicrograph demonstrates the two characteristic components of myelolipoma: mature adipocytes and hematopoietic tissue. D: H&E photomicrograph at higher magnification shows trilineage hematopoietic elements within the myelolipoma.

C) Photomicrograph (hematoxylin-eosin, 10x) revealing a neoplasm with two components, one of which consists of mature adipocytes mixed with hematopoietic components. D) Photomicrograph (hematoxylin-eosin, 40x) providing a closer view of the hematopoietic elements, with islands of erythropoiesis, myeloid precursors, and megakaryocytes being identified.

in_text_mentions: panese female patient presented with a left abdominal mass. She was referred to our surgical outpatient clinic to undergo a detailed examination and treatment for the left abdominal mass. A clinical examination revealed an elastic soft, smooth-surfaced, painless, child-head-sized tumor with poor mobility, which was located in the left upper abdomen. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a child-head-sized mass with heterogeneous contrast at the left upper abdomen around the stomach, spleen, pancreas, and left kidney on a horizontal image (Figure 1(a)) and coronal image (Figure 1(b)).

The retroperitoneal tumor was resected (Figure 3). The tumor was located at the left side of the stomach, posteriorly to the transverse mesocolon and pancreas, on the cranial side of the left kidney (Figures 1 and 2), but has not invaded the surrounding organs (Figures 1 and 2). The right adrenal gland was normal in size. The resected tumor was 20 × 18 × 10 cm in diameter and weighted 1500 g. An examination of the cut surface of the tumor revealed a multilobular yellow mass with bleeding in places (Figure 4).

in_text_mentions: In June 2020, a subsequent CT scan revealed no signs of disease but identified hepatic cystic lesions. In December 2020, two years post breast cancer diagnosis, a follow-up CT scan uncovered bilateral adrenal masses characterized by a heterogeneous and multicystic nature. The left mass measured 10x7.5cm, and the right mass measured 8x5cm (Figure 1), with the primary diagnostic considerations encompassing bilateral pheochromocytoma and potential metastatic deposits.

panels.attribution_text: Tyritzis et al. Giant adrenal myelolipoma, a rare urological issue with increasing incidence: a case report.. Cases journal 2009. doi:10.4076/1757-1626-2-8863. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Myelolipoma attached to the adrenal gland (H & E stain, ×25), (b) Typical hstological features of myelolipoma comprising adipose tissue and poorly differentiated plasma cells with large, hyperchromatic nuclei (H & E stain, ×100).
in_text_mentions: Surgery was performed through a right subcostal incision for the extraperitoneal approach of the right adrenal gland. The mass was totally dissected from the upper pole of the right kidney and excised en-block with the right adrenal gland. The macroscopic examination of the mass revealed a giant mass measuring 19 × 12 × 2 cm, surrounded by a thin capsule. Yellow adipose tissue was unevenly scattered on the capsule with varying amounts of red hematopoietic tissue (Figure 2). The pathology report showed a giant myelolipoma of the right adrenal gland.

in_text_mentions: med in at a level three hospital so as to ensure the presence of an intensive care unit due to the potential bleeding risk. The pathology report described a 4×7×6cm adrenal mass with a grey-yellow surface covered partially with a thick grey capsule with brown areas with a hemorrhagic and yellow adipose center. The microscopic evaluation showed an external layer of clear cortical cells of the adrenal granulosa; a center made of mature adipocytes and all three hematopoietic cell lines without calcifications or fibrosis. The final diagnosis was determined to be an adrenal myelolipoma ( Figure 3).

in_text_mentions: Macroscopic examination revealed a gray-yellow, encapsulated, irregularly shaped mass, 16.5 x 15 x 6.5 cm in size (Figure 4). On cut section, the tumor had fatty appearance and elastic texture. Microscopically, the tumor consisted of mature adipocytes admixed with hematopoietic components, including myeloid, erythroid and megakaryocytic elements (Figure 5). On tumor’s total periphery, there were sites of compressed, normal adrenal tissue, and this finding was similar to the intraoperative appearance of the tumor (Figure 6). These findings confirmed the diagnosis of AML.

The retroperitoneal tumor was resected (Figure 3). The tumor was located at the left side of the stomach, posteriorly to the transverse mesocolon and pancreas, on the cranial side of the left kidney (Figures 1 and 2), but has not invaded the surrounding organs (Figures 1 and 2). The right adrenal gland was normal in size. The resected tumor was 20 × 18 × 10 cm in diameter and weighted 1500 g. panels.rationale: Single real-patient plain abdominal radiograph from a case report on concurrent adrenal and extra-adrenal myelolipoma. The caption describes a well-defined low-density mass displacing the left kidney, which is a compatible manifestation of a large fat-containing myelolipoma. The article title provides disease focus, but the panel itself does not specify adrenal origin and could reflect the extra-adrenal component; attribution is therefore moderate.

Abdominal CT revealed a 24 × 16 × 22 cm solid mass with diffuse fat density originating from the right adrenal gland, starting from the left subdiaphragmatic region, extending to the pelvis, and filling the retroperitoneal area (Figure 3). It was causing compression in the inferior vena cava. The patient was diagnosed with adrenal myelolipoma (AML). The patient underwent open surgery, and an encapsulated mass weighing 4,229 g was removed. Histopathological examination reported that the mass contained a mixture of mature adipose tissue and myeloid tissue.

No other disease or third-party copyright is indicated.

in_text_mentions: Gross pathology revealed encapsulated, well-defined, soft masses measuring 11.5 × 8.5 × 6.0 cm, 15.0 × 10.0 × 6.5 cm, 6.0 × 5.5 × 3.5 cm, and 2.0 × 2.0 × 2.0 cm. Histologically, all the masses consisted of hematopoietic and mature fat tissue (Figure 3). The dominant tissue component was granulopoietic cells in various developmental stages, with the normal morphology of the megakaryocyte lines. There was no suprarenal gland tissue in the tumor, so the definitive diagnosis was extra-adrenal myelolipoma.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal CT of a real patient showing a fat-containing adrenal mass and a separate retroperitoneal mass, with caption confirming simultaneous adrenal and extra-adrenal myelolipoma. [raw subtype: simultaneous adrenal and extra-adrenal] B: Axial CT panel showing the extra-adrenal/retroperitoneal myelolipoma in the same patient; specific fat-containing mass is visible, although the vocabulary only names adrenal CT findings. [raw subtype: extra-adrenal/retroperitoneal] C: Additional axial CT panel of the extra-adrenal/retroperitoneal myelolipoma in a real patient; shows a fat-containing retroperitoneal mass, a variant location for myelolipoma. [raw subtype: extra-adrenal/retroperitoneal]
panels.attribution_text: Zieker et al. Simultaneous adrenal and extra-adrenal myelolipoma - an uncommon incident: case report and review of the literature.. World journal of surgical oncology 2008. doi:10.1186/1477-7819-6-72. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: CT imaging of the abdomen. A: Coronal abdominal CT scan detected two fat-containing masses in the adrenal gland and lateral of the psoas muscle inferior to the right kidney. Both lesions appeared identical in the CT imaging and were at first consistent with a well-differentiated liposarcoma. Intra-operative biopsy followed by rapid section revealed a simultaneous adrenal and extra-adrenal myelolipoma. B and C: Further CT images of the extra-adrenal/retorperitoneal myelolipoma.

The lesions were separate and had no connecting tissue in between them (Figure 1). To further confirm the obtained CT scan results an MR imaging was performed and showed again a fat-containing lesion in the adrenal gland and a 7 × 5 × 7 cm soft tissue-tumour inferior to the right kidney without invasion of the right kidney, urethra or renal vasculature. Both lesions appeared similar in the CT and MR imaging and were consistent with a well-differentiated liposarcoma (Figure 1

r a differentiation between an adrenal or extra-adrenal myelolipoma and other fat-containing retroperitoneal tumours can be difficult. The majority of fat-containing tumours are well-differentiated liposarcomas [20,21]. Since extra adrenal myelolipomas are histologically identical to their adrenal counterpart, the CT and MR findings should appear similar [2,22]. A fact that was proven in our case since both lesions appeared almost identical in the CT imaging (see Figure 1). Concerning the described case, at first an infrarenal metastasis or an adrenal and extra-adrenal liposarcoma was assumed.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Axial CT panel shows arrow-marked fat-containing retroperitoneal masses in a human patient, consistent with the caption's multiple retroperitoneal myelolipomas. The case is extra-adrenal/perirenal, so classified as a variant of the configured myelolipoma disease. b: Axial CT panel shows additional arrow-marked fat-containing retroperitoneal masses in a human patient, consistent with the caption's multiple retroperitoneal myelolipomas. The extra-adrenal/perirenal location makes this a variant presentation.
panels.attribution_text: Benko et al. Rare Case of Multiple Perirenal, Extra-Adrenal Myelolipoma: Case Report, Current Management Options, and Literature Review.. Case reports in urology 2021. doi:10.1155/2021/6614641. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: CT scan with multiple retroperitoneal myelolipomas (arrows).
in_text_mentions: Subsequent CT examination of the abdomen reviled four separate, extrarenal, well-circumscribed, round-shaped, and fat-containing retroperitoneal masses (12.0 × 12.0 cm, 12.0 × 8.0 cm, 6.0 × 3.5 cm, and 5.0 × 4.5 cm). Due to the volume of the masses, the aorta and inferior vena cava were compressed, as well as branches of the superior mesenteric artery. There was no hydronephrosis, and suprarenal glands and other organs appeared normal (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)). Based on the radiological findings, the initial differential diagnosis was liposarcoma.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E histology of a mediastinal myelolipoma showing adipose and hematopoietic tissue, consistent with myelolipoma; the article also describes an adrenal myelolipoma. The extra-adrenal location makes this a less common variant. B: High-power H&E shows mature adipose tissue admixed with hematopoietic cells, the classic histologic pattern of myelolipoma. Because the captioned lesion is mediastinal rather than adrenal, attribution to the configured adrenal_myelolipoma category is made as a location variant.

panels.rationale: Single axial CT image from a case of giant adrenal myelolipoma, showing a large heterodense right interhepatorenal mass with a fat-density hypodense component and tissue component; the caption and in-text description support the CT diagnosis.
panels.attribution_text: Sara et al. Too Massive and Too Atypical to Be Benign: The Unexpected Face of a Giant Adrenal Myelolipoma.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.101961. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Scannographic image of a large right interhepatic-renal mass
in_text_mentions: Abdominal ultrasound showed a hyperechoic tissue mass in the right adrenal gland, confirmed by an abdominal CT scan, which revealed a rounded, well-defined interhepatorenal mass heterodense with a hypodense component (-11UH) and a tissue component (30UH), slightly enhanced after contrast agent injection, measuring 9.4*11.2*12.6 cm, initially suggesting an adrenal origin. It comes into contact with the lower surface of the liver without any detectable fatty border. At the bottom, it exerts a mass effect on the ipsilateral kidney, with moderate effusion and peripheral calcifications (Figure 1).
